title: Apple Prepares Biggest Smart Home Push With Three New Devices and AI-Powered Siri at the Center
excerpt: The tech giant's HomePad display hub, indoor security camera, and a future robotic-arm model are all slated for launch, with Vietnam manufacturing marking a major shift in Apple's production strategy.
body:
• Apple is preparing to launch three new smart home devices, led by the HomePad, a 7-inch touchscreen hub with facial recognition, priced around $350
  • The HomePad hardware has been finished for months but was delayed repeatedly due to Apple's struggles to deliver an overhauled AI-powered Siri
  • Apple now targets a fall 2026 launch alongside iPhone 18 Pro and tvOS 27, after the device slipped from its original spring 2025 timeline
  • All three devices will be manufactured in Vietnam by BYD, breaking Apple's long-standing pattern of building first-generation products in China
  • A larger 9-inch version with a robotic arm is planned for 2027, alongside an indoor security camera expected as soon as late 2026

Apple's Smart Home Ambitions

Apple is finally making its most aggressive push into the smart home market. According to multiple reports, including detailed accounts from Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, the company is preparing to launch three new devices that would dramatically expand its home product lineup: a 7-inch touchscreen hub known internally as the HomePad, an indoor security camera, and a larger display with a robotic arm.

https://x.com/FirstSquawk/status/2082089655932240081

The cornerstone of the strategy is the HomePad, code-named J490, which represents Apple's first dedicated smart home display. The device features a 7-inch square touchscreen with a single USB-C port and Apple's signature silver aluminum finish. Users can mount it on a wall or place it on a half-dome-shaped speaker base that resembles a HomePod mini.

The home screen uses circular app icons arranged in a style similar to the Apple Watch interface, and the device is designed to serve as a centralized hub for controlling smart home devices, making FaceTime calls, playing music, and accessing glanceable information like weather and calendar events.

The Siri Problem

The HomePad's headline feature is an advanced facial recognition system that identifies household members as they approach, then surfaces personalized content — reminders, calendar events, notes, and music preferences — without any manual input. That kind of ambient, context-aware experience is precisely why the device has been stuck in limbo: it depends on a fundamentally more capable version of Siri that Apple has struggled to deliver.

Apple initially planned to ship the HomePad in spring 2025. When the revamped Siri was not ready, the timeline slipped to spring 2026. It slipped again when testing revealed that key AI features originally targeted for the iOS 26.4 update cycle would need to be pushed to iOS 26.5 and tvOS 27. The device is now expected to launch in the fall, likely in September alongside the iPhone 18 Pro.

The repeated delays underscore a broader challenge for Apple. The company announced ambitious AI capabilities for Siri nearly two years ago, including the ability to understand on-screen context and operate as a true conversational assistant. Much of that functionality remains undelivered, drawing criticism from analysts and consumers alike.

Manufacturing Shift to Vietnam

In a significant strategic move, all three smart home products are on track to be built in Vietnam by BYD — the Chinese electric vehicle and electronics manufacturer. This breaks with Apple's long-standing practice of building first-generation products in China before diversifying production to other countries.

The manufacturing shift reflects Apple's ongoing effort to reduce its dependence on Chinese production amid persistent US-China trade tensions. Apple has been steadily expanding its manufacturing footprint in India and Vietnam for existing product lines, but starting an entirely new product category outside China marks a notable escalation of that strategy.

The Competitive Landscape

Apple enters the smart home display market years behind Amazon and Google, both of which launched AI-powered home displays years ago. Amazon's Echo Show and Google's Nest Hub have established significant market positions, particularly in the United States.

However, Apple holds a powerful advantage in its installed base of more than 2.5 billion active devices globally, along with the deep integration of its ecosystem spanning iPhones, iPads, Macs, Apple Watch, and Apple TV. Apple's approach to privacy — with on-device processing and a commitment to not using home data for advertising — could also differentiate it in a market where privacy concerns around always-on microphones and cameras have grown.

The HomePad is expected to be priced around $350, positioning it well above the HomePod mini at $99 and closer to the full-sized HomePod at $299, but below the iPad mini at $499.

What's Next

Beyond the initial HomePad launch, Apple is reportedly developing a larger 9-inch version with a robotic arm, planned for 2027, that could move the display to track users as they move around a room. An indoor security camera is expected as soon as late 2026. The company is also working on AI-powered wearable accessories, including a camera-equipped version of AirPods and smart glasses — products that would depend on the same upgraded Siri that has proven so difficult to complete. For now, all eyes are on whether Apple can finally deliver its AI assistant in time for the September hardware launch.
nri_angle: Apple's Vietnam manufacturing shift has implications for India's aspirations to attract more Apple production; the smart home push affects the growing Indian Apple ecosystem
